vignette:
He is a 20-year-old African man who has already carried responsibilities that make him seem older than his age. By the time he comes to describe what happened, he has spent long shifts as a doctor in a combat setting, moving between triage tables and wounded bodies with a speed that leaves little room for thought. Before the trauma, he describes himself as disciplined and proud of his work, someone who believed that if he stayed focused enough, he could keep others alive and keep himself steady.

The event he returns to again and again begins on a day that starts like many others and ends with confusion, blood, and noise. He is working when the attack comes, and the sounds arrive before the full meaning does—gunfire, shouting, people running, the sudden collapse of routine. He remembers looking up from a patient and seeing the room change in an instant, as though the air itself has turned dangerous. As a doctor, he moves toward the injured out of training and habit, but that instinct is quickly tangled with fear. He tries to keep his voice calm while his body is shaking. He remembers pressure in his chest, the sharp awareness that every decision matters, and the helplessness of realizing there are too many wounded and not enough time.

In the chaos that follows, he sees deaths he cannot prevent. He describes one scene in particular with painful precision, as if the details are fixed in place: the sound of boots on the floor, the smell of smoke and metal, a colleague calling for help, someone’s hand slipping from his grasp. He keeps replaying the moment when he understands that the place where he worked, where he had expected to heal, can also become a place of immediate threat. Since then, he says, safety has not felt reliable anywhere. Even ordinary sounds can pull him back there. A door banging, a burst of shouting in the street, or the sudden crack of fireworks makes him freeze before he can tell himself where he is.

After the event, sleep becomes difficult and restless. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes quickly, alert to noises in the room or outside. He has nightmares that are not always exact repetitions of what happened, but they carry the same feeling of panic and urgency. In them, he is always arriving too late, always searching for someone he cannot reach. On waking, he often feels disoriented, with his heart racing and his body already braced for danger. He finds that he avoids talking about the attack unless he feels he has no choice, and even then his words come slowly. Certain images rise up in his mind without warning while he is trying to work, eat, or sit with other people.

He notices that his mind has become divided between the demands of his profession and the parts of him that remain stuck in that day. At work, he can still function, but it takes a great deal of effort. He double-checks equipment, watches exits, and scans rooms before settling in. He is more irritable now, especially when people move too quickly or ask questions while he is concentrating. He says he no longer feels as open with others, and even though he is single and has peers around him, he keeps a distance he did not used to need. He does not trust calm to last. When he is not working, he often feels empty and detached, as if his life has narrowed to surviving the next hour.

He also describes moments when he feels his body reacting before his thoughts can catch up: tight muscles, sudden sweating, a jolt of fear that seems too large for the situation. At times he becomes aware that he is holding his breath. He tries to stay busy because stillness leaves room for memories to enter. Even so, the memories come anyway, usually in fragments—faces, sounds, the weight of responsibility, the instant before he understood how vulnerable he was. He does not speak dramatically about the trauma. Instead, he describes it with the controlled tone of someone who has had to contain too much for too long, and beneath that control there is a persistent sense of alarm, grief, and fatigue that has not eased with time.
